title: The mobile visit for a small consultancy
metaTitle: The mobile visit for a small consultancy
excerpt: On a phone, the first screen has to name the problem and offer a working session. Do not let a desktop layout or an industry row decide that view.
alt: A bright office window ledge with a laptop, a closed notebook, white chairs, and a tall indoor tree, a calm wide scene that a phone crop can empty of the problem.
caption: A wide ledge looks complete until a phone crop removes the point. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What must the first phone screen show for a consultancy?
faqs.answer: The problem you take, and a way to book a working session, without scrolling. Keep the button label short enough for a thumb. Do not spend that screen on a row of industries or a second button for a download.

faqs.question: Which speed measures matter there?
faqs.answer: Google's good thresholds are a Largest Contentful Paint within 2.5 seconds, an Interaction to Next Paint within 200 milliseconds, and a Cumulative Layout Shift under 0.1. web.dev describes those as loading, responsiveness, and visual stability. A slow or jumpy hero spends the buyer's scarce hour on the page instead of the decision.

faqs.question: Should desktop be designed first?
faqs.answer: No. Stack the phone view first, then add space on the wide screen around the same words. A poster cropped down will hide the problem. If a headline only works on a large monitor, it is the wrong headline.

sources.title: Understanding Core Web Vitals and Google search results

markdown:
A small consultancy mobile website is where a buyer comparing you with their own time will judge you, often between the tasks they have been failing to finish. The first screen still has to show the problem you actually take and a way to book a working session. Do not let the desktop composition decide the phone page. A wide interior that crops the problem sentence into a fragment has already lost to the spreadsheet in their other hand.

Google's Core Web Vitals guidance sets three good thresholds: Largest Contentful Paint within 2.5 seconds, Interaction to Next Paint within 200 milliseconds, and Cumulative Layout Shift under 0.1. web.dev describes those measures as loading, responsiveness, and visual stability. On a phone they show up as whether the problem is there, whether the booking responds, and whether the page jumps while they read. A buyer who is protective of an hour will not wait through a lobby photograph to find out if you are worth that hour.

## The phone is the site

Start the layout at a narrow width. Write the problem so it fits in the first view. Put the session where a thumb can reach it. Then let the desktop add space around that stack. Shrinking a desktop poster is how the problem disappears and a tasteful room remains.

Open the page on a phone you did not design on. Read only what is visible before scrolling. You should be able to say the problem and see how to book. If either requires a scroll, the wide layout won. Cut the line that lists sectors if it pushes the problem down. A row of industries is especially expensive on a phone. It becomes the entire first screen, which is the failure in its most concentrated form.

A window ledge, a sofa, a tree in an office, can wait. The first screen is a sentence and an action. A picture can support them only if the subject survives the crop. If the meaningful part is at the edge, choose another frame or none. Type should be readable without pinching. Let the sentence wrap. A wrap is better than a line set for a desktop column that becomes a caption.

## The session in the first view

The button is "Book a working session," or the honest short form of it, visible with the problem. A link inside a closed menu is not enough. The label has to fit on one line. "Book a session" fits. "Schedule a strategic immersion" does not. The next screen can explain the hour. The button is the door.

Do not place a second button for a newsletter or a download beside it. On a phone, two buttons become the screen. The buyer is comparing you with doing the work themselves. A download looks like more homework. Give them the session. Put the essay in the footer if you must.

If the button sticks as they scroll, keep it short and do not let it cover the last line of a proof. Test on a small phone. The smallest screen is the one to design for, because that is where an hour feels most expensive.

Say the length of the session in the first view if you can do it in a few words. "90 minutes, you leave with the decision." That clause is the comparison with their calendar. Without it, the button is a meeting of unknown size, which is the kind they already dread.

## What to cut when the width shrinks

The phone page is not every desktop block made narrow. Cut, in this order. An industry row. An autoplay film of the office. A five-step method. An origin story above the problem. A logo wall. Keep the problem, the session, one picture that survives the crop, one refusal, and one path into a proof. The fee can be a sentence. Bios can be names and problems, not full essays before the button repeats.

Nielsen Norman Group's account still applies, often more on a phone: people leave within 10 to 20 seconds, and the first 10 are the judgment. Do not ask for patience. A buyer doing this between tasks will abandon a long scroll that has not named the problem.

Watch layout shift. If the headline jumps when a font arrives, or the button drops when an image loads, the page moved under their finger. Reserve space for the image. Google's good threshold for Cumulative Layout Shift is under 0.1. web.dev's description is the practical version: the page should stay still. You do not need to worship the score. You need the problem line to remain where the eye put it.

## Speed is part of the comparison

A slow first screen is a broken one. Largest Contentful Paint, good within 2.5 seconds, is the loading of the main content. If the hero is a huge photograph of a lounge, the phone downloads the wrong argument before it can show the problem. Use a lighter frame, or no frame, until the sentence is fast.

Interaction to Next Paint, good within 200 milliseconds, is what the booking button feels like. If a script delays the tap, they tap twice and decide the session is already a hassle. Keep the first view free of a carousel, a chat widget, and an animation that runs before the sentence is readable. Test on an ordinary connection. If a banner covers the button, rewrite the banner. The banner is not allowed to become the homepage.

## A review in one sitting

Hand a phone, locked, to someone who has the problem and has been doing it themselves. Ask them to unlock it and, within about ten seconds, say the problem and how they would book. If either answer fails, change the first screen before you discuss anything below. Then have them tap through and say whether the next screen matches. Rotate the phone. The sentence should still read. The button should still be tappable.

Repeat after visual polish. A new typeface or a larger logo will push the problem down. Write down the crop. If the artifact is missing, change the picture. Do not caption your way out of a bad crop. They will not read the caption in the first 10 seconds.

Ask them whether they would still do it themselves after seeing only that screen. If the answer is yes because the page looked like every consultancy, you still have a mood on the screen. Replace it with the problem. Their time is the competitor. The phone review is where that competitor wins or loses.

## The screen after the tap

The first screen can be right and the next screen can still lose them. On a phone, the booking view should repeat the problem, the length, and what they leave holding, in the same words. A naked calendar with a grid of times looks like every other meeting. The buyer who is comparing you with their own afternoon will close it. Put one sentence above the times: the decision they will leave with, and who must be present.

Do not ask them to create an account. Do not ask for a company size dropdown before they can pick a time. Those fields are a desktop CRM habit, and on a phone they are a wall. Name, a way to reply, and the problem if it is not already in the link. The rest can wait until the session is real.

If the only times you offer are next month, say so before they tap, not after they have scrolled a calendar of gray days. A delay you hide is the same delay they are already living. Honesty about the next open hour is part of the mobile page, because that is where the tap happens. If you have no hours, take the button off until you do. A button that dead-ends is worse than a sentence that says the books are closed until a date.

Check this flow with a thumb, not with a mouse on a resized browser window. The resized window lies about hit size and about what the keyboard does to the form. The keyboard will cover the button. The real phone will show you that. Fix the order of the fields until the button is reachable after the keyboard opens.

## The wide screen comes second

When the phone holds the problem and the session, the desktop can breathe. More of an artifact can show. A second column can hold a refusal. The menu can be a row. None of that may change the words. If the wide headline is clever and the narrow one is clear, ship the clear one in both places.

Do not keep two versions of the truth. One problem. One action. One picture subject. Ask them to find the fee shape on the phone without help. If it takes a hunt, the narrow site is still a poster. One sentence on the fee is enough. A fee that exists only at desktop width will be missed by the buyer who never opens a laptop to decide this.

After they can book from the phone, the next screen has to say what happens. Read [what the contact path should promise, and why ten fields lose them](/blog/a-contact-path-for-a-small-consultancy) before that button opens a long form.

If you want the first screen judged as a buyer would judge it, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the live page on a phone. A desktop screenshot hides the crop that matters.
